Every team knows the feeling: a project stalls because four people across three time zones can't find a two-hour window that works for everyone. Async meetings — short for asynchronous meetings — are the fix. Instead of gathering everyone at once, async communication lets team members contribute, respond, and move work forward on their own schedule. But async meetings only deliver results when they're run with intention. This guide covers eight async meeting best practices that help your team collaborate without the calendar chaos, keep decisions documented, and make sure nothing falls through the cracks.

## What is an async meeting?


An async meeting is a structured exchange of information, decisions, or feedback that happens without all participants being online at the same time. Instead of a scheduled video call, team members contribute using recorded video updates, shared documents, threaded discussions, or recorded audio notes — each on their own schedule, within an agreed deadline. Async meetings are popular with distributed and[remote teams](https://www.zoom.com/en/blog/small-business-ai/) because they remove the need to find a single shared meeting window across time zones, without sacrificing the structure or accountability of a real meeting.


## Async vs. synchronous meetings: when to use each


Not every conversation benefits from an async format. Here's a quick guide to help you decide:


Scenario Use async Use synchronous (live)


Sharing project status updates ✅


Collecting feedback on a document or proposal ✅


Sensitive HR or performance conversations ✅


Fast-moving decisions that need immediate answers ✅


High-energy creative brainstorming ✅


Cross-time-zone team standups ✅


Weekly status reporting ✅


Onboarding or relationship-building ✅


Reviewing and approving a deliverable ✅


The rule of thumb: if the conversation can wait hours for a thoughtful response, async is often the stronger choice. If it needs rapid back-and-forth or emotional nuance, schedule a live meeting instead.


## 8 async meeting best practices


### 1. Set a clear purpose and deadline before you start


Async meetings fail most often because the ask is vague. Before you post a video update or open a shared document for comment, define three things: What decision needs to be made? What specific input do you need from participants? When do you need it?


A clear purpose and a firm response deadline turn async communication from a passive information drop into a structured conversation with a finish line. Without a deadline, threads go cold. With one, contributors know exactly when to weigh in and you can move the work forward on schedule.


### 2. Give participants enough context to respond without back-and-forth


One of the biggest drains on async productivity is the follow-up question. When you share an update or request feedback, frontload all the context a participant needs to respond independently. That means linking to relevant documents, summarizing the background in the opening paragraph, and spelling out the exact type of input you're looking for — a decision, edits, ideas, or a simple acknowledgment.


This respects your teammates' time and keeps the thread from turning into a slow-motion chat that stretches over days.


### 3. Choose the right format — video, document, or thread


Async communication isn't one-size-fits-all. A few guidelines for matching format to content:


- **Short recorded video** works well for walkthroughs, demos, or anything where tone and context matter and text would lose nuance —[Zoom Clips](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/screen-recorder/) lets you record and share polished video updates directly within[Zoom Workplace](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/collaboration-tools/) , without switching to a separate tool.
- **Shared documents** work well for feedback rounds, proposals, and decisions that need a written record everyone can reference —[Zoom Canvas](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/collaborative-docs/) makes those docs collaborative, searchable, and built directly into Zoom Workplace, so nothing gets lost in email threads or separate platforms.
- **Threaded discussion** works for quick approvals, status checks, or yes/no decisions.
- **Recorded voice notes** work well for nuanced feedback where video isn't necessary.


Match the format to the complexity of the content. A two-sentence status update doesn't need a five-minute video.


### 4. Set response-time expectations upfront


Async doesn't mean "respond whenever." Clear response-time norms are what separate high-functioning async teams from ones where threads go cold for days. Be explicit in every post: "Please respond by Thursday at noon in your local time zone." If your team uses a shared channel, agree on a standing response window — within 24 hours on business days, for example — and document it somewhere every new teammate can find it.


Setting expectations upfront also creates psychological safety. Teammates know they won't be expected to reply instantly, which lets them give more considered, higher-quality responses.

### 5. Document decisions, not just discussions


This is where many async-first teams stumble. A rich discussion happens, a decision gets made — and then it lives in a thread nobody can find six weeks later. Effective async meeting best practices require a written decision log that's accessible, searchable, and shared with everyone who needs it.


After each async round, post a clear summary: what was discussed, what was decided, what the next steps are, and who owns each one. That summary becomes the source of truth. Anyone who missed the thread — or joined the project later — can get up to speed without hunting through chat history.


### 6. Keep video updates brief and focused


If you're using recorded video as your async format, aim for under five minutes. That's not a rigid rule, but it's a useful guardrail. Long recordings are hard to skim and easy to skip. Before you hit record, write a two-sentence outline of what you'll cover. If you find yourself going past the five-minute mark, that's often a signal the topic may be better suited for a live discussion.


Pair every video update with a written summary or a timestamped list of key points. Fast-moving teammates can skim the summary and jump to the sections most relevant to them — which increases the odds your update actually gets watched.


### 7. Assign a clear owner to every action item


An async meeting that ends with "someone should follow up on that" is an async meeting that ends in ambiguity. Every next step needs a name attached to it, a deadline, and a place where it's tracked. Whether your team manages tasks in a project management tool, a shared document, or a dedicated channel, the habit of naming owners in writing is what converts async discussions into finished work.


This is also where a reliable record of what was said — and what was decided — pays off. When the written record is clear, there's less room for "I thought you were doing that" moments. To learn more about how AI can help automate action item tracking,[see how small businesses are using AI agents](https://www.zoom.com/en/blog/build-ai-agent/) to handle post-meeting follow-up automatically.


### 8. Review and refine your async process regularly


Async communication habits drift. What worked for a five-person team starts to break down at 15 or 20. Build in a brief quarterly check-in — a synchronous one — to ask: Where are threads going cold? Are response deadlines realistic? Are we using the right formats for the right conversations? Is documentation actually being shared?


Treat your async process like any other team workflow: document it, share it with every new teammate, and adjust it when it stops serving the work.

## Frequently asked questions about async meeting best practices


### What is an async meeting?


An async meeting is a structured exchange of information or decisions where participants don't need to be online at the same time. Team members contribute using recorded videos, shared documents, or threaded discussions — each on their own schedule, within an agreed deadline. Async meetings are common with distributed and remote teams because they remove the need to find a single shared meeting window across time zones.


### What are the most important async meeting best practices for remote teams?


Start with a clear purpose and a firm response deadline, then provide all necessary context upfront so participants can respond without follow-up questions. Choose the right format for your content — video, document, or thread. After each round, document what was discussed, what was decided, and who owns each next step. That written record is what keeps an async process moving forward without constant check-ins.


### What's the difference between async and synchronous meetings?


Synchronous (sync) meetings happen in real time — everyone is present at the same moment, whether in person or on a video call. Asynchronous (async) meetings allow participants to contribute on their own schedule, within a set window. Sync works best for sensitive conversations, rapid creative back-and-forth, and situations where immediate decisions are needed. Async works best for updates, feedback rounds, approvals, and cross-time-zone collaboration.


### When should you not use async meetings?


Async isn't the right fit for every situation. Avoid it when a decision needs to happen within minutes, not hours. Sensitive conversations — performance reviews, conflict resolution, or emotional check-ins — benefit from the nuance of a live exchange. And when a topic needs rapid creative back-and-forth, a real-time brainstorm will move faster than an async thread.

Together, they help your team move work forward on its own schedule while keeping every decision documented and easy to find.


## Conclusion


Async meeting best practices don't require a complete overhaul of how your team works. Set a clear purpose, give enough context, document decisions, and assign owners — and your team can move work forward across any time zone without the scheduling chaos. Add a reliable way to capture what was said, and the async thread always has a foundation to build on.
